1.pericope_label: Og of Bashan defeated, his sixty cities taken, and his iron bedstead

schools.summary: Gill describes the country as fine for pasturage and famous for its oaks — the same which in Josephus is called Batanea. Calvin draws the inference from the sixty cities besides the villages: it shows both the extent of the country and the special help of God, in that they took in so short a time so many cities begirt with high walls, as if they were merely travelling through a peaceful land with nothing to do.

Henry makes Og's boldness the lesson of the campaign. He came out against Israel to battle, and it was wonderful that he did not take warning by the ruin of Sihon and desire conditions of peace; but he trusted to his own strength, and so was hardened to his destruction — those not awakened by the judgments of God upon others, but persisting in their defiance of heaven, are ripening apace for the like judgments upon themselves. Of the bedstead he reckons both ways: you might guess at Og's weight by the material, iron, as if a bedstead of wood were too weak for him to trust to, and at his stature by the dimensions, for supposing a cubit half a yard it was four yards and a half long, and allowing the bedstead two cubits longer than himself he was three yards and a half high, double the stature of an ordinary man — yet they smote him, and when God pleads his people's cause he can deal with giants as with grasshoppers.

Clarke supposes the verse on the names of Hermon to have been a marginal remark which afterwards got incorporated with the text, or an addition by Joshua or Ezra. On the bedstead he sets the cubit at eighteen inches and makes Og twelve feet, noting that commentators who lengthen the bedstead and shorten the man still leave him nine; and he complains that on this subject the rabbins have trifled most sinfully. His specimen is the Targum of Jonathan, where Og tears up a mountain six miles at its base to throw on the camp, but a worm bores a hole so that it falls about his shoulders while his teeth grow out and stick fast in it, and Moses, himself ten cubits high, takes an axe ten cubits long and leaps ten cubits to strike him on the ankle. Wesley explains the several names of Hermon as given to one mountain partly by several peoples and partly in regard of its several tops; and of the bedstead he asks how it came to Rabbath, answering either that the Ammonites took it as spoil in some former battle, or that after Og's death they desired the monument and the Israelites let them carry it away.

Keil derives the name Bashan from the soil, the Hebrew word signifying a soft and level ground, whence the Greek Batanaea; Argob he traces to the stony district now called the Leja, covered with heaps of large blocks of stone. Ellicott will not follow Clarke on the Hermon verse: it would not be safe to assert that the mention of the Sidonian name makes it an addition from after Israel was in Palestine, though it might be so; there are several notes of this kind in the Pentateuch. On the bedstead he doubts the object itself: the word may mean bedstead or coffin, and an iron bedstead and an iron coffin are almost equally improbable; basalt has been suggested, but though there is basalt in Argob there is none at Rabbath. He prefers Conder's discovery there of a remarkable stone throne on a hillside, since the Hebrew word properly signifies a couch with a canopy and the word for iron means a prince in Talmudical language, so that the sense would be, his canopied throne was a princely one and yet remains in Rabbath — the dimensions of that throne being nearly those given here.

12.pericope_label: The conquered land divided among Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh

schools.summary: Calvin explains why the grant is rehearsed at all. Since this territory had fallen to the two tribes and a half exceptionally, the matter might be brought into controversy with posterity, and so Moses declares again that they were its rightful possessors. And because the gift itself might be questioned, the land lying outside the bounds of the promised inheritance, he anticipates that objection too by asserting that God had not in vain given it to be possessed. Lest so unequal a partition should become a subject of contention, he marks their boundaries on every side, as though he set up the authority of God as a wall and rampart against any who should presume to invade it. On the names he gives the ancient ones their equivalents — the Dead Sea is here the Sea of Salt, the Lake of Gennesaret Chinnereth — and declines to make Ashdoth-Pisgah the name of a city, as some do. Gill agrees with Wesley that Gilead was given not to Machir himself, who cannot be thought living then, but to his posterity.

Henry observes the subdividing of Manasseh: Joseph was divided into Ephraim and Manasseh, Manasseh into one half on each side of Jordan, and the eastern half again into the families of Jair and Machir. He reads the phrase the land of the giants as a memorial rather than a description: it is so called because it had been in their possession, though Og was the last of them, and they were rooted out sooner than any of their neighbours — for those who, presuming upon their strength, had their hand against every man, had every man's hand against them, and went down slain to the pit, though they had been the terror of the mighty in the land of the living. He closes on the terms attached to the grant, that they were to send a strong detachment over Jordan to lead the van and not return to settle until they had seen their brethren in as full possession as themselves: they must be taught not to look at their own things only but at the things of others, since we are not born for ourselves but are members one of another.

Wesley disputes the rendering of the boundary. Half the valley is rather to the middle of the river, since the word translated half commonly signifies middle, and the same Hebrew word means both a valley and a brook; and this agrees with the fact, for as that river was the border, one half of it belonged to them and the other to their neighbours. He points out that our translators render the very same Hebrew words elsewhere from the middle of the river, in a passage describing these same bounds. Of the closing note on Jair's cities he says it must be put among the passages not written by Moses but added by the men who digested his books into this order. Clarke glosses the name: Bashan-havoth-jair is Bashan of the cities of Jair.

Keil sets out the division: the southern portion, from Aroer in the Arnon valley and half Gilead as far as the Jabbok, went to Reuben and Gad, and the northern half of Gilead with all Bashan to the half-tribe of Manasseh — and Argob was not merely one portion of Bashan but identical with it, so far as it belonged to Og's kingdom. On the disputed boundary he reaches Wesley's reading by grammar, taking the phrase for a more precise definition of the Arnon valley: their territory was not to reach merely to its northern edge but into the middle of it, as far as the river which flowed through. Ellicott says the closing words about Jair's cities point to a later hand, as of Joshua describing the completion of the conquest, the expression unto this day being characteristically common in that book.

18.pericope_label: The two tribes and a half charged to go armed, and Joshua encouraged

schools.summary: Gill limits the address: it was directed not to all Israel but to Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, since what follows concerns only them. He dates the charge to Joshua after the conquest of the two kings and the assignment of their countries, and after Moses had been told that he should quickly die and Joshua succeed him; and he names what they were not to fear, neither the numbers and gigantic stature of the inhabitants, nor their walled towns. Calvin states the bargain the command enforced: Moses had introduced an agreement that the two tribes and a half should not enjoy their possession until they had accompanied their brethren in the subjugation of Canaan, so that he had given them a place not where they were at once to settle themselves, but where they might deposit their wives and cattle until the whole people were peaceably established. Of the charge to Joshua he says in a word that Moses exhorted him and the whole people to prepare to occupy the land with alacrity, relying as well upon God's promise as upon the numerous proofs of his assistance already given, which were so many pledges of the future continuance of his grace.

Henry makes the encouragement of Joshua a duty of age toward youth: those aged and experienced in the service of God should do all they can to strengthen the hands of those who are young and setting out in religion. Two things he would have Joshua consider: what God has done, and what God has promised. Of the first, Joshua had seen with his own eyes what a total defeat God gave by the forces of Israel to these two kings, and might infer not only that thus the Lord can do with all the rest, for his arm is not shortened, but that thus he will do, for his purpose is not changed — he that has begun will finish; and the more we have seen of divine wisdom, power and goodness, the more inexcusable we are if we fear what flesh can do unto us. Of the second, that cause cannot but be victorious which the Lord of hosts fights for; and we reproach our leader, Henry says, if we follow him trembling. On the prayer that follows he notices when it came: at the very time when Moses was encouraging Joshua, and taking it for granted that Joshua must be their leader, he was touched with an earnest desire to go over himself, and that desire expressed itself not in passionate complaints or reflections upon the sentence he was under, but in humble prayer that it might graciously be reversed — for we should never allow desires in our hearts which we cannot in faith offer up to God by prayer. Henry sets out the two pleas. The first is the experience Moses had already had of God's goodness: thou hast begun to show thy servant thy greatness, therefore perfect what thou hast begun; and the more we see of God's glory in his works, the more we shall desire to see. He asked not to be a prince and a ruler there, being content to resign the government to Joshua, but only to see the good land. The second is the impression those works had made — what God is there in heaven or in earth that can do according to thy works? — from which Henry infers that those shall see the works of God who admire him in them.

Wesley reads the phrase all that are meet for the war as leaving the number to the others' judgment; and he supplies the figures, that these tribes were in all above a hundred thousand, of whom forty thousand went over Jordan before their brethren.
Keil finds the weight of the promise in the grammar, the pronoun being emphatic and adding force to the subject: it is Jehovah himself who will fight for them.

23.pericope_label: Moses prays to cross over, is refused, and charges Joshua instead

schools.summary: Calvin reads the verb as a pluperfect: Moses interrupts himself to show why he resigned his office to another, since it is not probable that after substituting Joshua he straightway conceived a contrary desire. The drift of the prayer, he says, is that God should fill up the measure of his grace, Moses enumerating the blessings already vouchsafed him as the ground of his confidence, that God, who is not wont to forsake the work of his own hands, might carry to the end the mercies begun. Of the goodly mountain he subscribes to those who understand Zion by it, since with the exception of Lebanon there was no other mountain so delectable in the land, and Lebanon is named second as if next in rank. On the refusal he rejects the notion that God was offended by the longing itself, holding that Moses is giving the reason why he did not obtain what he sought, that he had been already excluded; and though he does not enter into debate with God, as if unjustly condemned for the faults of others, he does indirectly reflect upon the people, since it was well they should all be reminded that the punishment inflicted upon God's distinguished servant was incurred by the guilt of them all. Gill puts the motive of the prayer plainly: the conquest of the two kings was the pledge and earnest of what God had promised, and Moses was desirous of living to see the work completed. He takes the beginning of the greatness for the beginning of God's power in vanquishing the Canaanites, and looks back to Meribah for the refusal — the Lord was wroth not at this time nor for this prayer, but because he and Aaron had not sanctified him at those waters, and for unadvised words the people's provocation drew from him.

Clarke renders the words of the refusal literally, there is an abundance to thee — thou hast had honour enough already and mayest well dispense with going over Jordan; he has no reason to complain who is taken from earthly felicity to heavenly glory, and in this God showed Moses both his goodness and his severity. Wesley reports the Jewish view of the goodly mountain, that they not improbably understood it of the mountain on which the temple was to be built, which Moses calls that mountain emphatically, as one much in his thoughts though not in his eye. Of the succession he makes the same point as Clarke's typology: it was not Moses but Joshua, whose name is Jesus, that was to give the people rest; and it is a comfort to those who love mankind, when they are dying and going off, to see God's work likely to be carried on by other hands when they are silent in the dust.

Keil refers the expression begun to show thy greatness not so much to the mighty acts in Egypt and at the Red Sea as to the manifestation of divine omnipotence in the defeat of the Amorites, by which the Lord had begun to bring his people into possession of the promised land. Of the goodly mountain he denies that any particular portion of Canaan is meant, whether the mountains of Judah or the temple mount, taking it for the whole land regarded as a mountainous country, Lebanon being named as the boundary wall toward the north. Ellicott gives Rashi's paraphrase of the refusal from older commentators, far more than this is reserved for thee, plentiful goodness is hidden for thee — and observes that so it proved, for on a goodly mountain Moses and Elias afterwards stood with the Saviour of the world and spoke of a conquest far more glorious than Joshua's, the exodus he should accomplish at Jerusalem.
